frames.narration: The user opens the app. It makes one request for the home screen and sends its version, the ETag of the last screen it showed, and its sync token for the lists. It has already drawn the saved screen from the phone's storage.

The version rules say that version 3 shows four parts, so the BFF starts all four calls at the same moment, each with its own timeout: profile 120 ms, orders 150 ms, recommendations 100 ms, promotions 80 ms.

Three services answer quickly: profile after 35 ms, orders after 62 ms and promotions after 28 ms. Recommendations is having a bad day and has not answered. The BFF keeps waiting only until its 100 ms timeout.

At 100 ms the recommendations call is cut off, since it is an optional part. The BFF looks in the cache and finds a copy from 6 minutes ago, and uses it, marked as stale. The screen time is the slowest allowed call, 100 ms, plus a few milliseconds to assemble.

The BFF trims every part to the fields that version 3 draws, about 6 KB where the services returned about 70 KB between them, computes an ETag, and answers after roughly 105 ms. The app draws the fresh parts and shows the recommendations as slightly old.
Twenty seconds later the user returns to the home screen. The app sends its new ETag, e52. The assembled screen is still in the cache, with a 30-second time to live, and its hash is unchanged.
Nothing changed, so the BFF answers 304 with no body. It made no backend call and sent a few hundred bytes. The app just keeps what it is showing.

A push notification brings two million people to the app within a minute. They all need today's promotions, which are the same for everyone. The BFF merges the waiting requests into one call, so the promotions service sees one request instead of thousands.

Two days later the user opens the app after a long flight. The app sends its sync token, t812. The change feed has 37 changes since then, such as orders that shipped and new inbox messages, and returns only those with a new token, t850, instead of the full lists.
